content_voiceover: These two board questions test how you manage inhibitor development in hemophilia A. In the first case, a forty year old man with mild hemophilia A, baseline factor eight around fifteen to twenty percent, sails through an appendectomy with a single prophylactic dose, but then develops new bruising and wound bleeding with his factor eight level crashing to under one percent. That pattern, a good response followed by a sudden loss of factor coverage, is the classic tip off for a new inhibitor. So the correct workup is to check the factor eight inhibitor titer, and once bleeding needs treatment you bypass the missing factor entirely using recombinant factor seven a or activated prothrombin complex concentrate, both of which work downstream of factor eight. What is not appropriate is jumping straight to inhibitor eradication with steroids and cyclophosphamide, since standard eradication for hemophilia inhibitors is immune tolerance induction with high dose factor concentrate, not empiric immunosuppression. The second question flips this around and asks you to spot the false statement about inhibitor epidemiology, reminding you that roughly thirty percent of previously untreated severe patients can develop an inhibitor, most cases cluster within the first twenty exposure days, prophylaxis and avoiding danger signals like same day vaccination can lower risk, and severe disease carries higher inhibitor risk than moderate or mild disease.
keypoints: Sudden loss of factor coverage after prior good response suggests a new inhibitor
Confirm with inhibitor titer, then bypass with rFVIIa or APCC for bleeding
Steroid plus cyclophosphamide is not standard inhibitor eradication
About 30% of severe hemophilia A patients develop inhibitors, mostly within 20 exposure days
Severe disease and danger signals like same-day vaccination raise inhibitor risk
keypoint_voiceover: Key takeaways here. A sudden drop in factor level after a prior successful exposure should make you suspect a new inhibitor, so check the titer. Treat active bleeding with bypassing agents, recombinant factor seven a or A P C C, not with immunosuppressants like steroids and cyclophosphamide, which are not standard eradication therapy. And remember the epidemiology, about thirty percent of severe patients develop inhibitors, most within the first twenty exposure days, and severity of disease plus danger signals such as same day vaccination both raise the risk.
